A Trusted Source

By: Harri Vithi | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What's in your syrup?

Unique Selling Point:
One of South Africa's largest pharmaceutical companies is accused of failing to comply with good manufacturing processes.

Summary:
Adcock Ingram is a Proudly South African company, and a leading South African pharmaceutical manufacturer. Founded over 130 years ago in 1891, the Company is listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange and its extensive portfolio of products includes well-known household brands like Panado, Allergex, Epi-max, Citro-Soda and Myprodol.

Adcock’s annual turnover as at June 2025 was 9.8 billion.

In October a whistleblower approached Carte Blanche with numerous concerns regarding the efficacy of Adcock’s manufacturing processes.
He didn’t come empty-handed; he had receipts including videos, pictures, emails and documents that if proven true - could be explosive allegations against Adcock.
He’s a qualified pharmacist and his role on the manufacturing floor was to ensure that the processes followed were aligned with Adcock’s standard operating procedures.
In short, he says - they didn’t.

Despite numerous complaints to the site manager - who he says is a non-professional with a logistics background - the whistleblower says, there was repeatedly pushback with a view to maximizing output over compliance.

Last month, fatigued with his incessant insistence on compliance which slowed down production, the whistleblower says he was dismissed for being a workplace bully and unofficially, a whistleblower who allegedly once declared - “Ive closed down factories before”. An allegation he dismisses as absolute drivel.


Further information:
In order of appearance:
This is a spray gun that is used to add flavour onto the final Citro-Soda powder before transferring to packaging. So the liquid within the assembled gun can be in contact with the flavourant raw material during spraying. The standard here is usage of stainless steel components that will be corrosion resistant
A damaged conveyor belt which has direct contact with production materials
Broken walls with peeling pain endorsed by the compliance manager as suitable for manufacturing in order to please production heads
Brown leaks from the roof while manufacturing Citro-Soda
Damaged conveyor belt in direct contact with product during manufacturing
The steam mixer pipe Adcock refused to fix until the whistleblower refused to run production which lead to victimization

This is a link to all videos and pictures:-
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1U_n__fSRLjy4Z2pjt-BEEBu8mfWex_iS?usp=drive_link

Most of these images and videos were taken in Adcock’s Citro Soda production area where the whistleblower last worked. He says up until a month ago this remained the status quo. Last year when SAHPRA (the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority) ranan audit, the Responsible Pharmacist deliberately ordered a deep clean so the auditor couldn’t access the area on the day. Allegedly, this is because Adcock knew Citro-Soda production wouldn’t have passed the audit. Notably, these manufacturing conditions are not limited to the production of Citro-Soda.

Interviews:

Whistleblower - hidden identity


Independent Pharmacy Production Specialist
We need to interview an independent pharmacy production specialist - perhaps an academic to review the pictures and videos as a backstop

SAHPRA - Their audits and standards

Adcock Ingram - ROR

Visual Treatment

VO: It's a renowned pharmaceutical company trusted by many...

VIZ: ( List all sorts of ailments on the screen till it's filled with words)
(Then the video of the fogged up manufacturing room... Silence for a second...)

VO: But behind the pristine packaging, some say its manufacturing processes may be taking a gamble with people's lives.

VIZ: Can we create fog or hire fog for the opening scene of this interview to mimic the conditions he worked in.
As the fog clears the camera zooms in on the gloves... The protective foot gear... The overcoat.

UPSOUND WHISTLEBLOWER : I worked in conditions like this...where the factory space would completely fog up. Can you imagine processing medications in a room where you can barely see?

VO: Can you imagine consuming medications manufactured in a foggy room?

UPSOUND WHISTLEBLOWER: This is one of the largest pharmaceutical companies in South Africa. Walk into any pharmacy and several of their products are available to you. That's the scary part.

Press Release:


I N V E S T I G A T I O N 
A Trusted Source
Allegations of faulty ventilation, rusting equipment, and poor cleaning standards. What’s going on inside this leading pharmaceutical company? It’s an old and well-respected local company, trusted to produce household pharmaceutical brands. But a whistleblower claims that, behind closed doors, manufacturing standards are slipping. From damaged conveyor belts to ventilation so poor, dust obscures visibility on the production line, the allegations are explosive. Carte Blanche investigates.
Producer: Harri Vithi | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


A Trusted Source

(Claire) We’ve all popped a pill for a headache or sipped on some syrup for a sore throat. We make the choices based on tried and tested brands but have you ever stopped to wonder how the medicines you trust are being manufactured?

(Claire) This cannot be acceptable.

(Whistleblower) It is not acceptable.

(Claire) Excuse me?

(Claire) Falling from…

(Whistleblower) That have been falling from the air handling unit.

(Claire) That is unbelievable. That is unbelievable. OK, I have no words.

(Claire) What is that?

(Claire) This is a story about a trusted pharmaceutical company accused of bypassing manufacturing standards in order to push production to the limit.

(Claire) And you’re probably familiar with its name.


(Claire) What pharmaceutical company are we talking about?


(Whistleblower) We're talking about Adcock Ingram Healthcare.

(Claire) Medical manufacturing happens behind closed doors. But this man spent days and nights on the production floor at Adcock Ingram.
(Whistleblower) My area of speciality is pharmaceutical manufacturing and I'm a registered pharmacist.

(Claire) You won’t see his face because he’s a former employee disclosing what he claims is sensitive information which could compromise his career.
(Whistleblower) My role on the production floor is to ensure that pharmaceutical manufacturing is conducted in GMP compliant areas. GMP is essentially a regulation to ensure safety and efficacy of the products that are being manufactured.
(Claire) GMP stands for Good Manufacturing Practice. In simple terms, GMP is our guarantee that we can trust the products we’re buying. It’s at the very centre of this story.
(Claire) Why did you decide to speak out?


(Whistleblower) There is such a flagrant violation of the very GMP, which really concerns me as a healthcare worker.


(Claire) But if what our source says is true, it’s not a story that should concern only healthcare workers.


(Claire) Adcock Ingram is a renowned pharmaceutical company that’s been around for more than a hundred years. It was started in a small pharmacy in Krugersdorp, just west of Johannesburg in 1890.

(Claire) Today, it’s the name behind the household brands that can be found on shelves in every supermarket and pharmacy.


(Whistleblower) Some of the most common brands is Citro-soda,cough syrups like your Alcophyllex, your Broncleer, Corenza C, Bioplus Effervescent Tablets. Panado syrups - Mayogel for example.


(Whistleblower) A company that declares 9.8 billion Rands in the last financial year.

(Claire) His primary concern is with this product: Citro-Soda Lemon Flavour - sold over the counter for the relief of urinary tract infection symptoms, heartburn and indigestion.

(Claire) Our source supplied this CCTV footage of the Citro-Soda Lemon Flavour Blending facility - seen here during a break in production. It’s at the company’s Clayville factory, on Joburg’s East Rand. These images show it looking pristine.

(Claire) In full production it is alleged to resemble a cement factory.

(Claire) What am I seeing?

(Whistleblower) So this process basically ensures that the particle size of the raw materials are of equivalent dimensions.

(Whistleblower) Above him, is the extraction system that is supposed to be protecting him from the fumes that are coming from the powder.

(Claire) This cannot be acceptable.

(Whistleblower) It is not acceptable.

(Claire) Our source claims the extraction system meant to remove possibly hazardous airborne contaminants—such as dust, fumes and vapors - didn’t work.

(Claire) This is how they are expected to work under these conditions?

(Whistleblower) So the eventuality of that becomes breathing problems and management has not bothered.

(Claire) These messages on a WhatsApp group intended for reporting issues show that the problem was first reported in July 2024. In August and October the next year, it appears repairs were needed again.

(Claire) These are serious allegations, so we went in search of an independent expert, but none of the local experts we approached were willing to go on the record. Instead, we interviewed Gareth Kilian, a South African now lecturing in Australia. He’s also a certified Good Manufacturing Practice lead auditor.

(Gareth Kilian) I'm a registered pharmacist with the South African Pharmacy Council. I've been a pharmacist for over 20 years.

(Claire) Good Manufacturing Practice classifies deviations based on the risk they pose to product quality or patient safety, ranging from MINOR to CRITICAL, in the most serious cases.

(Claire) A critical finding is not necessarily life threatening for a consumer but does indicate that the product may be compromised.

(Gareth Kilian) The video evidence was quite alarming.

(Gareth Kilian) It's not toxic material by any means, but it has the potential to cause irritation in the lungs. So that is a health and safety concern, but also it's a concern for potential cross-contamination.

(Claire) Cross-contamination means Citro-Soda particles could unintentionally mix into another medication, posing health risks for some patients.

(Claire) Adcock Ingram declined an interview, but in a series of letters, the company insists that all our source’s allegations are baseless and have never been reported at the Clayville site.

(Claire) It says Citro-Soda is manufactured in dedicated facilities with a special air handling unit that controls any risk of cross-contamination, and staff must change into dedicated protective equipment before they enter. They deny their extraction system is not functional

(Claire) Killian says, if what Adcock Ingram says is correct, the GMP deviation classification would be minor. However, he says a faulty air handling unit would impact the effectiveness of the controls Adcock Ingram describes.

(Claire) Killian says the risk to the workers remains, despite their protective equipment.

(Gareth Kilian) So companies are required to have very strict maintenance in order to ensure that all their equipment is in good working order at all times.

(Claire) Adcock Ingram sent us this manufacturing licence for its Clayville facility, dated June 2025, claiming that it proves any compliance issues had been resolved by then.

(Claire) However, SAHPRA told us it completed its audit of the facility and granted the licence in March. And most of our evidence dates from after Adcock’s license was granted.

(Operations Manager) As discussed on the phone earlier, I've spoken to QA [quality assurance] regarding this complete cleaning.

(Claire) We’re told this recording is of the Operations Manager.

(Operations Manager) So today we're not going to do complete cleaning.

(Operations Manager) What we're trying to do is that we want to try and clean every Saturday. So, irrespective of whether we do two batches or five batches or whatever the number of batches during the week, it doesn't matter.

(Claire) Our source says this violates procedure, which requires cleaning after a fixed and known number of batches have been processed.

(Whistleblower) So he wants to maximize the number of batches that you can manufacture in that room without cleaning.

(Claire) The cleaning instructions appear again in this email from a concerned production pharmacist - four months later.

(Claire) Adcock Ingram denied all wrongdoing and says their cleaning procedures are effective. Killian says that, if operators were formally instructed to clean less often than regulations dictate, that would be classified as a critical violation.

(Claire) Back to the Operations Manager:

(Operations Manager) The leaking from the ceiling might come again

(Operations Manager) With that brown stuff because currently we don't know where it's coming from.

(Claire) The “brown stuff” can be seen in this video from our source.

(Whistleblower) So at times because of these non-cleaning procedures these are debris of previous crystallized components of the product.

(Claire) Falling from …

(Whistleblower) That have been falling from the air handling unit directly onto the product.

(Claire) Excuse me?

(Whistleblower) So that is highlighting how crucial your ventilation and air conditioning system is.

(Claire) Yes.

(Gareth Kilian) It looked like this yellow viscous liquid, which could potentially be harboring microorganisms or other contaminants.

(Gareth Kilian) That would be critical, because it's directly contaminating the product.

(Claire) Adcock Ingram claims that the liquid may possibly be the result of high-pressure cleaning before manufacturing and says the environmental monitoring data shows no microbial risk.

(Claire) If Adcock Ingram is right and the liquid was dried before production began, there would be no violation of GMP. But this email suggests that the substance did drip onto the working production line.

(Claire) In any case, Adcock Ingram say they are investigating different cleaning techniques to enhance the cleaning process.

(Whistleblower) This is a conveyor belt it's essentially just disintegrating.

(Claire) The conveyor belt transfers Citro-Soda from the crushing section to where flavour is added.

(Claire) Those are not supposed to be there, right?

(Whistleblower) Yes, ma'am.

(Whistleblower) That product is actually at risk,

(Whistleblower) And also it's white and the bulk product is white.

(Claire) White.

(Whistleblower) And you are therefore faced with the situation where - we can only hope.

(Claire) I don't want to only hope when I'm buying.

(Claire) Adcock Ingram told us that the conveyor belts are inspected regularly and replaced if necessary. The company also says that the finished product is inspected hourly during packaging, and a quality control laboratory rejects any product that doesn’t meet specifications.

(Claire) But Killian points out that the amount of disintegration visible in the videos indicates prolonged wear and tear. He says he wouldn’t expect the white particles to be picked up in the check described.

(Claire) Is that a serious non-compliance issue?

(Gareth Kilian) It is critical; it's in fact a little bit more concerning because it's more difficult to detect.

(Claire) In this CCTV footage operators are not on a break: production was allegedly halted by pharmacists to demand replacement of rusty equipment, specifically this steam mixer pipe.

(Whistleblower) It is not acceptable by GMP standards to actually be having oxidized equipment within the manufacturing space.

(Claire) Our source says that, for a prolonged period - after SAHPRA’s inspection - pharmacists haggled with management to get rusty equipment replaced.

(Claire) Equipment like this spray gun septum, which adds lemon flavour to the Citro-soda: in other words it was in direct contact with the product.

(Gareth Kilian) So, equipment. rusting, it could potentially cause contamination of the product with rust and other metal particles.

(Gareth Kilian) There were other videos and photographic evidence that showed black particulate rust particles that were present in the final product and that is a critical nonconformity for GMP.

(Claire) Killian says if rust gets into the product, that could cause digestive problems or even heavy metal toxicity.

(Claire) Despite these internal communications, Adcock Ingram claims that black particles have never been observed or reported in any Citro Soda batches, which it says undergo extensive quality checks.

(Claire) Eventually, both the steam mixer pipe and the spray gun were replaced.

(Claire) Adcock Ingram says rust is “unlikely” to have been seen in its facility, but these communications suggest otherwise.

(Claire) The company did tell us they have invested in changing machine parts to rust resistant stainless steel.

(Claire) The regulator - SAHPRA declined an interview and denied our request for a copy of Adcock Clayville’s audit reports saying, it can’t legally share them.

(Claire) How transparent is the pharmaceutical industry when it comes to addressing issues of non-compliance?

(Gareth Kilian) South Africa has got a way to go in terms of making the public aware of the potential hazards that companies are putting them under.

(Claire) Adcock Ingram say they take compliance and patient safety seriously, and conducted their own audit of the Clayville facility after receiving our questions. The company sent us extracts of the report which they say found no evidence of systemic GMP non-compliance.

(Claire) But if what our source says is true, it’s not a story that should concern only healthcare workers. (Claire) Adcock Ingram is a renowned pharmaceutical company that’s been around for more than a hundred years. It was started in a small pharmacy in Krugersdorp, just west of Johannesburg in 1890. (Claire) Today, it’s the name behind the household brands that can be found on shelves in every supermarket and pharmacy. (Whistleblower) Some of the most common brands is Citro-soda,cough syrups like your Alcophyllex, your Broncleer, Corenza C, Bioplus Effervescent Tablets. Panado syrups - Mayogel for example. (Whistleblower) A company that declares 9.8 billion Rands in the last financial year. (Claire) His primary concern is with this product: Citro-Soda Lemon Flavour - sold over the counter for the relief of urinary tract infection symptoms, heartburn and indigestion. (Claire) Our source supplied this CCTV footage of the Citro-Soda Lemon Flavour Blending facility - seen here during a break in production. It’s at the company’s Clayville factory, on Joburg’s East Rand. These images show it looking pristine. (Claire) In full production it is alleged to resemble a cement factory. (Claire) What am I seeing? (Whistleblower) So this process basically ensures that the particle size of the raw materials are of equivalent dimensions. (Whistleblower) Above him, is the extraction system that is supposed to be protecting him from the fumes that are coming from the powder. (Claire) This cannot be acceptable. (Whistleblower) It is not acceptable. (Claire) Our source claims the extraction system meant to remove possibly hazardous airborne contaminants—such as dust, fumes and vapors - didn’t work. (Claire) This is how they are expected to work under these conditions? (Whistleblower) So the eventuality of that becomes breathing problems and management has not bothered. (Claire) These messages on a WhatsApp group intended for reporting issues show that the problem was first reported in July 2024. In August and October the next year, it appears repairs were needed again. (Claire) These are serious allegations, so we went in search of an independent expert, but none of the local experts we approached were willing to go on the record. Instead, we interviewed Gareth Kilian, a South African now lecturing in Australia. He’s also a certified Good Manufacturing Practice lead auditor. (Gareth Kilian) I'm a registered pharmacist with the South African Pharmacy Council. I've been a pharmacist for over 20 years. (Claire) Good Manufacturing Practice classifies deviations based on the risk they pose to product quality or patient safety, ranging from MINOR to CRITICAL, in the most serious cases. (Claire) A critical finding is not necessarily life threatening for a consumer but does indicate that the product may be compromised. (Gareth Kilian) The video evidence was quite alarming. (Gareth Kilian) It's not toxic material by any means, but it has the potential to cause irritation in the lungs. So that is a health and safety concern, but also it's a concern for potential cross-contamination. (Claire) Cross-contamination means Citro-Soda particles could unintentionally mix into another medication, posing health risks for some patients. (Claire) Adcock Ingram declined an interview, but in a series of letters, the company insists that all our source’s allegations are baseless and have never been reported at the Clayville site. (Claire) It says Citro-Soda is manufactured in dedicated facilities with a special air handling unit that controls any risk of cross-contamination, and staff must change into dedicated protective equipment before they enter. They deny their extraction system is not functional (Claire) Killian says, if what Adcock Ingram says is correct, the GMP deviation classification would be minor. However, he says a faulty air handling unit would impact the effectiveness of the controls Adcock Ingram describes. (Claire) Killian says the risk to the workers remains, despite their protective equipment. (Gareth Kilian) So companies are required to have very strict maintenance in order to ensure that all their equipment is in good working order at all times. (Claire) Adcock Ingram sent us this manufacturing licence for its Clayville facility, dated June 2025, claiming that it proves any compliance issues had been resolved by then. (Claire) However, SAHPRA told us it completed its audit of the facility and granted the licence in March. And most of our evidence dates from after Adcock’s license was granted. (Operations Manager) As discussed on the phone earlier, I've spoken to QA [quality assurance] regarding this complete cleaning. (Claire) We’re told this recording is of the Operations Manager. (Operations Manager) So today we're not going to do complete cleaning. (Operations Manager) What we're trying to do is that we want to try and clean every Saturday. So, irrespective of whether we do two batches or five batches or whatever the number of batches during the week, it doesn't matter. (Claire) Our source says this violates procedure, which requires cleaning after a fixed and known number of batches have been processed. (Whistleblower) So he wants to maximize the number of batches that you can manufacture in that room without cleaning. (Claire) The cleaning instructions appear again in this email from a concerned production pharmacist - four months later. (Claire) Adcock Ingram denied all wrongdoing and says their cleaning procedures are effective. Killian says that, if operators were formally instructed to clean less often than regulations dictate, that would be classified as a critical violation. (Claire) Back to the Operations Manager: (Operations Manager) The leaking from the ceiling might come again (Operations Manager) With that brown stuff because currently we don't know where it's coming from. (Claire) The “brown stuff” can be seen in this video from our source. (Whistleblower) So at times because of these non-cleaning procedures these are debris of previous crystallized components of the product. (Claire) Falling from … (Whistleblower) That have been falling from the air handling unit directly onto the product. (Claire) Excuse me? (Whistleblower) So that is highlighting how crucial your ventilation and air conditioning system is. (Claire) Yes. (Gareth Kilian) It looked like this yellow viscous liquid, which could potentially be harboring microorganisms or other contaminants. (Gareth Kilian) That would be critical, because it's directly contaminating the product. (Claire) Adcock Ingram claims that the liquid may possibly be the result of high-pressure cleaning before manufacturing and says the environmental monitoring data shows no microbial risk. (Claire) If Adcock Ingram is right and the liquid was dried before production began, there would be no violation of GMP. But this email suggests that the substance did drip onto the working production line. (Claire) In any case, Adcock Ingram say they are investigating different cleaning techniques to enhance the cleaning process. (Whistleblower) This is a conveyor belt it's essentially just disintegrating. (Claire) The conveyor belt transfers Citro-Soda from the crushing section to where flavour is added. (Claire) Those are not supposed to be there, right? (Whistleblower) Yes, ma'am. (Whistleblower) That product is actually at risk, (Whistleblower) And also it's white and the bulk product is white. (Claire) White. (Whistleblower) And you are therefore faced with the situation where - we can only hope. (Claire) I don't want to only hope when I'm buying. (Claire) Adcock Ingram told us that the conveyor belts are inspected regularly and replaced if necessary. The company also says that the finished product is inspected hourly during packaging, and a quality control laboratory rejects any product that doesn’t meet specifications. (Claire) But Killian points out that the amount of disintegration visible in the videos indicates prolonged wear and tear. He says he wouldn’t expect the white particles to be picked up in the check described. (Claire) Is that a serious non-compliance issue? (Gareth Kilian) It is critical; it's in fact a little bit more concerning because it's more difficult to detect. (Claire) In this CCTV footage operators are not on a break: production was allegedly halted by pharmacists to demand replacement of rusty equipment, specifically this steam mixer pipe. (Whistleblower) It is not acceptable by GMP standards to actually be having oxidized equipment within the manufacturing space. (Claire) Our source says that, for a prolonged period - after SAHPRA’s inspection - pharmacists haggled with management to get rusty equipment replaced. (Claire) Equipment like this spray gun septum, which adds lemon flavour to the Citro-soda: in other words it was in direct contact with the product. (Gareth Kilian) So, equipment. rusting, it could potentially cause contamination of the product with rust and other metal particles. (Gareth Kilian) There were other videos and photographic evidence that showed black particulate rust particles that were present in the final product and that is a critical nonconformity for GMP. (Claire) Killian says if rust gets into the product, that could cause digestive problems or even heavy metal toxicity. (Claire) Despite these internal communications, Adcock Ingram claims that black particles have never been observed or reported in any Citro Soda batches, which it says undergo extensive quality checks. (Claire) Eventually, both the steam mixer pipe and the spray gun were replaced. (Claire) Adcock Ingram says rust is “unlikely” to have been seen in its facility, but these communications suggest otherwise. (Claire) The company did tell us they have invested in changing machine parts to rust resistant stainless steel. (Claire) The regulator - SAHPRA declined an interview and denied our request for a copy of Adcock Clayville’s audit reports saying, it can’t legally share them. (Claire) How transparent is the pharmaceutical industry when it comes to addressing issues of non-compliance? (Gareth Kilian) South Africa has got a way to go in terms of making the public aware of the potential hazards that companies are putting them under. (Claire) Adcock Ingram say they take compliance and patient safety seriously, and conducted their own audit of the Clayville facility after receiving our questions. The company sent us extracts of the report which they say found no evidence of systemic GMP non-compliance.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: One of South Africa's largest pharmaceutical companies is accused of failing to comply with good manufacturing processes.
metadata.Summary: Adcock Ingram is a Proudly South African company, and a leading South African pharmaceutical manufacturer. Founded over 130 years ago in 1891, the Company is listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange and its extensive portfolio of products includes well-known household brands like Panado, Allergex, Epi-max, Citro-Soda and Myprodol. Adcock’s annual turnover as at June 2025 was 9.8 billion. In October a whistleblower approached Carte Blanche with numerous concerns regarding the efficacy of Adcock’s manufacturing processes. He didn’t come empty-handed; he had receipts including videos, pictures, emails and documents that if proven true - could be explosive allegations against Adcock. He’s a qualified pharmacist and his role on the manufacturing floor was to ensure that the processes followed were aligned with Adcock’s standard operating procedures. In short, he says - they didn’t. Despite numerous complaints to the site manager - who he says is a non-professional with a logistics background - the whistleblower says, there was repeatedly pushback with a view to maximizing output over compliance. Last month, fatigued with his incessant insistence on compliance which slowed down production, the whistleblower says he was dismissed for being a workplace bully and unofficially, a whistleblower who allegedly once declared - “Ive closed down factories before”. An allegation he dismisses as absolute drivel.
metadata.Further information: In order of appearance: This is a spray gun that is used to add flavour onto the final Citro-Soda powder before transferring to packaging. So the liquid within the assembled gun can be in contact with the flavourant raw material during spraying. The standard here is usage of stainless steel components that will be corrosion resistant A damaged conveyor belt which has direct contact with production materials Broken walls with peeling pain endorsed by the compliance manager as suitable for manufacturing in order to please production heads Brown leaks from the roof while manufacturing Citro-Soda Damaged conveyor belt in direct contact with product during manufacturing The steam mixer pipe Adcock refused to fix until the whistleblower refused to run production which lead to victimization This is a link to all videos and pictures:- https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1U_n__fSRLjy4Z2pjt-BEEBu8mfWex_iS?usp=drive_link Most of these images and videos were taken in Adcock’s Citro Soda production area where the whistleblower last worked. He says up until a month ago this remained the status quo. Last year when SAHPRA (the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority) ranan audit, the Responsible Pharmacist deliberately ordered a deep clean so the auditor couldn’t access the area on the day. Allegedly, this is because Adcock knew Citro-Soda production wouldn’t have passed the audit. Notably, these manufacturing conditions are not limited to the production of Citro-Soda. Interviews: Whistleblower - hidden identity Independent Pharmacy Production Specialist We need to interview an independent pharmacy production specialist - perhaps an academic to review the pictures and videos as a backstop SAHPRA - Their audits and standards Adcock Ingram - ROR Visual Treatment VO: It's a renowned pharmaceutical company trusted by many... VIZ: ( List all sorts of ailments on the screen till it's filled with words) (Then the video of the fogged up manufacturing room... Silence for a second...) VO: But behind the pristine packaging, some say its manufacturing processes may be taking a gamble with people's lives. VIZ: Can we create fog or hire fog for the opening scene of this interview to mimic the conditions he worked in. As the fog clears the camera zooms in on the gloves... The protective foot gear... The overcoat. UPSOUND WHISTLEBLOWER : I worked in conditions like this...where the factory space would completely fog up. Can you imagine processing medications in a room where you can barely see? VO: Can you imagine consuming medications manufactured in a foggy room? UPSOUND WHISTLEBLOWER: This is one of the largest pharmaceutical companies in South Africa. Walk into any pharmacy and several of their products are available to you. That's the scary part.
